posts.hook: Every December, our oven gets booked before our calendar does.
alt_hooks: Holiday baking starts weeks before the holidays.
Small bakery, big December: here's how we plan it.
posts.caption:
Every December, our oven gets booked before our calendar does.

Running a small bakery in the holiday season is mostly a planning exercise: how much flour, how many hands, how many hours of slow fermentation we can fit between now and the 24th. We'd rather tell you our limits early than sell out of your plans late.

So from today, holiday pie and bread preorders are open until December 20, with pickup December 22–24.

If you're planning a team breakfast or a client thank-you, message us — we'll tell you honestly what we can make well.

posts.hook: This loaf took longer to make than your last vacation.

This loaf took longer to make than your last vacation. (Okay, maybe not. But it feels like it.)

Watch till the crust crackles. Send it to the friend who still buys sliced bread. 😉

posts.topic: Why we refuse to rush our dough (small-business lesson)
posts.research_rationale: Text-led owner posts suit LinkedIn's preference for native content over external links (S6) and support owner-profile amplification (S7).
posts.hook: The most expensive ingredient in our bread is time.
alt_hooks: Our slowest process is our best business decision.
What slow dough taught me about growth.
posts.caption:
The most expensive ingredient in our bread is time.

We could make sourdough faster. Plenty of shortcuts exist. But the slow fermentation is where the flavour and the crust come from, and it's the reason people come back.

That's been the biggest lesson of running a small business: the things you can't rush are usually the things that make you worth choosing.

In December that means we cap preorders rather than cut corners. It's a harder sell, and a better promise.

What's the 'slow ingredient' in your business?

posts.topic: Lessons from a holiday rush: capacity, honesty and neighbours

posts.hook: Three things a holiday rush teaches a small bakery.
alt_hooks: What December taught us (again).
A small-business year-end reflection.
posts.caption:
Three things a holiday rush teaches a small bakery:

1. Say your limits out loud early. Capping orders protects quality and the team.
2. Logistics are part of the product. A clear pickup plan matters as much as the pie.
3. Neighbours notice effort. [Owner: add one real moment from pickup week before posting.]

Thank you to everyone who ordered, shared, or just stopped in for coffee. On to the new year — slowly, as always.

— Maya

posts.topic: Why we score our bread (the slash explained)
posts.research_rationale: Process content earns watch time and sends (S5); a satisfying 'why' explainer fills the education gap vs. competitors (competitor research; S21).
posts.hook: That slash on top of your bread isn't decoration.
alt_hooks: Why bakers cut their loaves before baking.
One cut, a lot of science.
posts.caption:
That slash on top of your bread isn't decoration. (Okay, it's a little bit decoration.) 🔪🍞

Scoring gives the loaf a controlled place to expand in the oven, so it rises where we want it to instead of bursting wherever it likes. Each baker's pattern is a bit like a signature.

Which score is your favourite — 1, 2 or 3? Comment below.
